reading.rtitle: Speaker Training Pack -- Transcript 04: Market Risk Update to the Executive Committee (recorded, 9 min 40 s)
paras: Editor's note. We put this transcript in the pack because of how little of it is decoration. Claudia Ferraz had a ten-minute slot and used nine minutes and forty seconds of it. There are almost no fillers in the recording: where most of us say a small empty sound, she takes a short pause instead, and the delivery is slower than people expect from somebody who is nervous. She does not digress once. And out of roughly forty sentences, only three carry any emphasis at all -- everything else is said flat, on purpose. Read it as a piece of engineering, not as a piece of writing.

"Ten minutes. What you have to decide today is one thing: whether the alert rollout starts in September, or whether it waits for October. Everything else in this pack is here because you may ask for it. I will give you the four lines and their dates, then the one risk that moves them, then my request. If I am still talking at nine minutes, stop me -- I would rather stop early than overrun and take the credit desk's slot.

"Line one, the deputy control: closed, signed last Tuesday, nothing outstanding. Line two, the alert: it goes live desk by desk from the first of September, and the risk desk is first. Line three, the quarterly number: confirmed on the twenty-ninth, and I will not read a provisional figure to this committee before then. Line four, the audit review: the fourth of November, nine in the morning, already in the diary. One aside, and then I am straight back on the plan -- three of you were in the room in July, and I know how this sounded then. It was the manual step that failed, not the model. The model produced the right number on the right morning and nobody ran it. I am saying that here because the note in July did not say it clearly enough, and I would rather correct it in front of you than let it sit.

"Back to the dates. What changed this quarter was the lead time, and nothing else: six weeks instead of two, because Risk Systems is carrying eleven changes. That single number is why line two cannot move to August, however much I would like it to. So, my request, and this is where I finish. I am asking you to approve September for line two, and to leave line four where it is. What I am not going to do is promise you a date I do not control -- I commit to the first milestone and not to the last one, and you will have the confirmed figure on the twenty-ninth. That is the decision I need from you today."

vocabmatch.title: Eight words from the transcript
vocabmatch.hint: Tap a word, then tap its meaning
defs: an empty sound or word you make while you are thinking
to come back to a point you left earlier, on purpose
to speak for longer than the time you were given
a short remark outside the main line, signalled and then closed
the amount of time you are given to speak
the extra weight you put on the words that matter most
the way you speak: pace, pauses and voice, not the content
to leave your main line and start talking about something else

listenings.text: Sergio, it is Marina. Ten minutes on Tuesday, and there are three things I want in your head before you stand up. First, write eight minutes of material, not ten. Everybody speaks slower standing up than they do at a rehearsal, and the room forgives a thin minute at the end. What it does not forgive is overrunning, because the four minutes you take are not yours; they come out of whoever is speaking after you, and that person will remember it. Second, and this is the one that changes how the ten minutes sound. Decide, before you write anything, which three sentences you want them to repeat to somebody else afterwards. Three. Build those three so that the important part lands at the end, and say everything else flat, on purpose. If you put weight on the fourth one, it cancels the first three, and the room stops hearing any of them. Third, the last sentence. Write your closing remark before you write the nine minutes in front of it, because that is the sentence they carry out of the room. And never end with that is it, or with any questions. End with the thing you are asking them to approve, said in full, and then be quiet and let them answer.

Sergio, Paulo here, from the credit desk. Two things about how it actually goes in that room, and neither is about grammar. The first one is the pause. When you need two seconds to find the next idea, you have a choice: make a small empty sound, or say nothing. It is the same two seconds either way, but a filler sounds like a man looking for a word, and silence sounds like a man who has decided something. Nobody has ever thought less of a presenter for pausing. The second one is the interruption, and this is where most people lose the ten minutes. Somebody will cut in halfway through with a question about the model. Do not follow them. Answer in one line, say out loud that you are coming back to it, finish the point you were on, and then circle back. If you abandon the line you were on, you will not find it again with eight people watching you. And an aside is fine, but say that it is one and close it in a sentence. If you digress without telling anybody, the room walks off the plan with you, and when you come back nobody can tell which part was the plan and which part was the story.

extra_audio.text: First, open with what the room has to decide today, and put the decision at the end of the sentence. Then walk through the lines of the plan with one date next to each of them. Next, correct the one thing the room has wrong, picking that part out with it was and that. After that, take the interruption in one line, finish the point you were on, and circle back. Finally, land on the closing remark you wrote before the rest, and then stop talking.
